articles.title: Inside Bengaluru's house of horrors: Mutton curry invite, sleeping pills, TV at full blast, bodies in gunny bags
articles.summary: BENGALURU: A dinner invitation, sleeping pills and a television blaring at full volume allegedly formed part of a chilling sequence of events leading to
articles.body: BENGALURU: A dinner invitation, sleeping pills and a television blaring at full volume allegedly formed part of a chilling sequence of events leading to seven murders at a rented house in Rajajinagar.Police suspect that a 52-year-old cab driver, S Indushekhar, killed his wife and six members of her extended family over a 15-day period before wrapping their bodies in plastic sheets, stuffing them into gunny bags and ferrying them in his car to different locations.The latest development in the case came with the recovery of the bodies of Indushekhar's wife Sunitha and her mother Rupavathi from a forest area in Salem district of Tamil Nadu. This has taken the total number of bodies recovered to three. A 12-member team comprising family members has travelled to Salem to identify the bodies and complete the necessary legal formalities.According to cops, Indushekhar allegedly killed Sunitha on the night of October 14. The following day, his 17-year-old daughter called Rupavathi and invited her to their home for dinner, saying they would prepare mutton curry. Investigators suspect the invitation was part of a plan to lure her to the house, where she was allegedly killed.During interrogation, Indushekhar allegedly told police that he used sleeping pills to sedate his victims before bludgeoning them with a grindstone after they fell asleep. He would turn up the television volume while attacking them to ensure that neighbours did not hear the sounds of the assaults, police said.After the killings, Indushekhar and his daughter allegedly wrapped the bodies in multiple layers of plastic sheets to prevent blood from leaking out before placing them in gunny bags. They would then carry the bags to his Toyota Etios in the early hours and drive away to dispose of the bodies at different locations.Police have recovered at least half a dozen perfume bottles from the Toyota Etios, which is now part of the investigation. Investigators are examining their possible use in connection with the disposal of the bodies.Also read: Bengaluru family massacre: Accused's daughter 'assisted' him at every stage of killings, say copsGold ornaments removed before bodies were dumpedInvestigators have also found that Indushekhar allegedly removed gold ornaments from the bodies of his wife and three other women before disposing of them. He is suspected to have sold some of the jewellery, and police are now trying to trace the transactions and establish where the ornaments went.The postmortem report of seven-year-old Puneeth, who was allegedly killed on October 29, confirmed four blunt-force injuries to his head, including the forehead and crown, police said.The 52-year-old cab driver was arrested near Ulsoorgate on Wednesday. Police suspect he killed seven people at his rented house on 59th Cross, Rajajinagar V Block, between October 14 and 31. The victims included his wife and six members of her extended family.His 17-year-old daughter is suspected to have assisted him in some of the murders and in disposing of the bodies. Investigators are probing her alleged role in the sequence of killings and the subsequent disposal of the victims.10-year-old boy was next targetA 10-year-old boy, the son of two of the victims, was found in Indushekhar's car when police arrested him near Ulsoorgate. Investigators said the accused had allegedly planned to kill the child as well.The boy had reportedly been taken away from his home on the pretext that his parents had gone on a pilgrimage. He spent several days with Indushekhar and his daughter, unaware that his parents had allegedly been murdered. Police suspect that the accused was waiting for an opportunity to kill him before his arrest.The boy's presence in the car proved crucial in the investigation, with police rescuing him before the alleged plan could be carried out.Nearly 20 years of marital discord behind killingsPolice suspect the murders stemmed from a prolonged marital dispute between Indushekhar and Sunitha. During questioning, he allegedly told investigators that he had been in conflict with his wife for nearly 20 years and blamed her relatives for supporting her during their disputes.Investigators are also examining the family property angle. Relatives of the victims have alleged that a dispute over property worth around Rs 3 crore could have been behind the killings, though police are continuing to establish the motive.The case came to light after family members grew suspicious when several relatives went missing. A relative had also noticed that messages were being sent from Sunitha's phone, but nobody was receiving calls from her.Investigators suspect Indushekhar had been using his wife's phone to message her mother and conceal her murder.Police are continuing to investigate the circumstances of all seven murders, the disposal of the bodies at different locations, the suspected sale of gold ornaments and the role of the accused's daughter.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Delhi AQI remains 'very poor' at 364; several areas record 'severe' levels as strict GRAP Stage-III curbs remain active
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi continued to reel under hazardous air pollution on Saturday morning, with the city's average Air Quality Index (AQI) recorded at 364 at 8
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi continued to reel under hazardous air pollution on Saturday morning, with the city's average Air Quality Index (AQI) recorded at 364 at 8 am, placing it in the 'very poor' category, according to data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).While the overall AQI showed a marginal improvement from Friday's reading of 389, authorities have allowed schools to shift primary classes to a hybrid mode, combining physical and online learning, under Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP). Several monitoring stations across the capital, however, continued to record 'severe' air quality.IIT Delhi recorded the highest AQI at 443, followed by Punjabi Bagh at 433 and Narela at 409. Cantonment Area registered an AQI of 315, while Dhaula Kuan recorded 318. Anand Vihar, meanwhile, reported an AQI of 272, placing it in the 'poor' category.Misty conditions prevailed at New Delhi's Safdarjung station in the early hours of Saturday, with the temperature recorded at 17 degrees Celsius at 5.30 am, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).The readings came a day after the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) invoked Stage III of GRAP across Delhi-NCR, two days ahead of Diwali, amid forecasts of further deterioration in air quality.Under the GRAP framework, an AQI of 301-400 is classified as 'very poor', while readings between 401 and 500 fall in the 'severe' category. The four-stage emergency plan is implemented in Delhi and adjoining districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, based on pollution and weather forecasts issued by the IMD and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM).With Stage III restrictions now in force, measures under the earlier stages will continue, alongside additional curbs aimed at reducing vehicular emissions, construction dust and industrial pollution.What Stage III restrictions meanThe restrictions include a ban on BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel four-wheelers in Delhi and designated NCR districts. Curbs have also been tightened on older light and medium goods vehicles, as well as non-Delhi-registered diesel commercial vehicles entering the capital.All non-essential construction activities involving high dust generation, including excavation, earthwork, demolition and road construction, have been suspended. Essential projects allowed to continue will have to follow stringent dust-control measures.Stone crushers and mining activities, which contribute significantly to particulate pollution, will also face shutdowns or operational restrictions.To discourage the use of private vehicles, authorities have also been directed to augment public transport services by increasing Metro frequency and deploying additional buses.Four stages of GRAPGRAP is a four-stage emergency framework implemented by the CAQM in coordination with the CPCB and state governments. Restrictions become progressively stricter depending on the severity of air pollution.Stage I is triggered when AQI ranges between 201 and 300, categorised as 'poor'. Measures include controlling road dust, enforcing pollution norms and preventing open waste burning.Stage II comes into force when AQI is between 301 and 400, or 'very poor'. It includes intensified dust-control measures, higher parking fees and staggered office timings.Stage III is implemented when AQI reaches 401-450, classified as 'severe'. It entails restrictions on polluting vehicles, a halt to non-essential construction activities and the option of hybrid classes for primary school students.Stage IV, or 'severe plus', is triggered when AQI crosses 450. It includes restrictions on heavy goods vehicles and additional emergency measures targeting traffic and industrial emissions.The latest restrictions are aimed at preventing air quality from deteriorating further and entering the 'severe plus' category. By targeting major sources of pollution, including particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10, as well as nitrogen oxides, the measures seek to reduce the risk of respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses.Authorities have stressed the need for coordinated action across the NCR, even as the emergency curbs remain in place. articles.summary: Ordinary pet dogs in Germany are being trained to take on an unusual conservation mission, sniffing out invasive plants before they spread further into
articles.body: Ordinary pet dogs in Germany are being trained to take on an unusual conservation mission, sniffing out invasive plants before they spread further into the wild. Researchers associated with the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research have found that volunteer dog-handler teams can be trained to identify specific invasive plant species using their powerful sense of smell. The project involved 31 teams that underwent training between 2021 and 2023, with 12 eventually completing field assessments. Of those, 11 passed the tests, achieving an average detection success rate of 75%. The findings highlight how everyday pet owners and their dogs could become additional participants in ecological monitoring and help conservationists locate invasive vegetation.How German researchers trained pet dogs to detect invasive plantsThe research was conducted as part of the IGAMon-Dog project, which explored whether privately owned dogs and their volunteer handlers could contribute to monitoring invasive alien species.Researchers trained the participating dogs to recognise the odours of three invasive plant groups: Himalayan balsam, common ragweed and knotweeds. The programme focused on teaching dogs to distinguish the target plants through scent rather than relying on visual identification.The training took place between 2021 and 2023 and involved 31 dog-handler teams. Participants were guided through structured exercises designed to help dogs recognise specific plant odours and communicate their findings to their handlers.The initiative brought together dog owners, trainers and environmental researchers to explore a citizen-science approach to invasive species monitoring.11 of 12 volunteer teams pass field testsThe field assessments provided an opportunity to evaluate whether the dogs could apply their training outside controlled exercises.Of the 31 teams that initially participated, 12 completed the field testing, and 11 successfully passed the assessment. The teams recorded an average detection success rate of 75%.The findings demonstrated that volunteer dog-handler teams could identify target invasive plants in real-world environments. The results also highlighted the potential of involving privately owned dogs in conservation work rather than depending exclusively on professionally trained detection animals.The difference between the number of teams initially trained and those that completed field testing also reflected the practical challenges involved in preparing volunteers and their dogs for this specialised work.Dogs use their noses to locate plants without disturbing themAn important part of the training involved teaching dogs how to communicate their discoveries without damaging the vegetation.Rather than digging up or biting the plants, the dogs were trained to give their handlers a passive indication when they detected a target scent. This allowed the volunteers to identify the location of a plant while leaving it undisturbed.The approach is particularly useful for ecological monitoring because the purpose is to locate and record invasive vegetation, not remove it during the search.Dogs' strong sense of smell gives them a potential advantage when searching areas where plants may be difficult to distinguish visually or are growing among other vegetation.Invasive alien species are considered one of the major drivers of biodiversity loss worldwide. They can spread into new environments, compete with native species and alter ecosystems.Identifying these plants at an early stage can give conservationists a better opportunity to control their spread. However, monitoring large natural areas requires considerable time, labour and resources.Researchers noted that the lack of effective early-detection methods has made it difficult for ecologists to identify new infestations before invasive species become established.Trained detection dogs could provide an additional way to survey these areas. Their ability to locate specific plant odours may help researchers identify target species even when visual searches are challenging.Everyday dog walks could become conservation missionsOne of the project's most interesting possibilities is the involvement of ordinary pet owners in biodiversity conservation.With appropriate training, volunteers could potentially incorporate invasive plant searches into their regular outdoor activities with their dogs. This could expand the number of people participating in ecological monitoring and help conservation groups gather information about where invasive plants are growing.The researchers highlighted the opportunity to combine dogs' sense of smell with the enthusiasm of citizen scientists. However, they stressed that successful monitoring requires carefully designed training and continued guidance from both dog-training and ecological experts.The project also developed recommendations for improving volunteer selection, coordination, dog training and the initial deployment of detection teams, which could help similar programmes become more effective.A citizen-science project backed by German research fundingThe initiative was part of the IGAMon-Dog project, which explored how trained dogs and volunteer handlers could contribute to monitoring invasive alien species.The research was led by Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth and colleagues at Germany's Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ). articles.title: Parliament restoration delays 'frustrating', says Commons Speaker
articles.summary: Sir Lindsay Hoyle urges action after a committee warns it is "crunch time" for the ailing building.
articles.body:
The Speaker of the House of Commons has expressed "frustration" with the lack of progress on restoration to protect the Palace of Westminster.

Sir Lindsay Hoyle told the BBC the current process for approving essential renovations to Parliament amounted to "putting ourselves in handcuffs", and said more time was spent "doing surveys" than getting repairs under way.

The Commons public accounts committee this week warned it was "crunch time" for the ailing building's restoration, which could cost up to £40bn and take 61 years.

It said every additional year of delay cost taxpayers £420m, while its chairman warned the Palace could be left vulnerable to a devastating fire like that which engulfed the Notre Dame.

Sir Lindsay said his "biggest frustration" with the Victorian building's restoration was that "we're not getting on with the work".

"We spend more time doing surveys," he told BBC Radio 4's The Week in Westminster . "Instead of doing surveys, why don't we start repairing the building?"

The Speaker criticised current legislation which means the main renovations cannot begin until Parliament has approved the entire project's scope and funding.

"It's very frustrating when the Act of Parliament prevents you carrying out the major repairs that you need to. Talk about putting ourselves in handcuffs."

He added: "What we have to do is renovate and repair the problems areas."

More asbestos found in Parliament, as MPs urged to get on with revamp

Parliament revamp could cost £40bn and take 61 years

Sir Lindsay also questioned why a fire-suppressing mist system had not yet been introduced throughout the building, even though he has called for it for years.

"The major part and the most historic parts of the building haven't got it, and that's what we need."

Asked about reports that Parliament might be given an opportunity to vote on the way forward before the end of 2026, Sir Lindsay said that was a matter for government business managers.

"Who knows when it's going to come forward? Let's see what the House decides," he said.

Much of the 19th-Century building's network of wires and pipes dates back to the 1940s - and some to the Victorian era - according to a report which warned of an "impending crisis" a decade ago. Fire safety issues and high levels of asbestos have also been identified.

The BBC understands government whips have discussed holding a debate and vote by the new year, but no date has been scheduled.

This would decide whether to proceed with up to £3bn of initial works and narrow down four current options, ahead of a final decision by 2030.

One proposed option would see MPs and peers move out of the site for up to 24 years from 2032, costing up to £15.6bn.

Another involves moving only the House of Lords out of the building, costing £39bn and taking 61 years.

The chairman of the body in charge of refurbishing Parliament defended the potential costs earlier this year , telling the BBC: "We're already spending £150m a year trying to keep the thing standing."

articles.title: U.S. military carries out new limited strikes on Iran
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said the U.S. military on Friday carried out new limited strikes on Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said the U.S. military on Friday carried out new limited strikes on Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system. Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the crucial waterway for oil shipments. Trump in an exchange with reporters described the military action as “minor." “They knocked out — they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," Trump told reporters shortly after arriving in West Palm Beach, Florida, on Friday evening. Trump did not offer further details about the target. But U.S. officials have reported that most of Iran’s air defense systems were destroyed or severely degraded during a June 2025 bombardment by Israel and in the early stages of the current conflict. U.S. officials have assessed that Iran would try to rebuild them and other military infrastructure over time. The U.S. military also reported carrying out what it described as defensive strikes on Monday. Explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. Friday's strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican Party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the U.S. The electoral setback — Republicans lost both chambers of Congress — was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the conflict and elevated fuel prices, a byproduct of the war that’s affected nearly every sector of the global economy. In the days since Republicans' shellacking at the polls, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near. Nuclear program reward U.S. Central Command, which oversees U.S. military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the United States was offering “a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above.” The post included a link to the State Department’s Rewards for Justice program. Differences with Iran over its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the more than 8-month-old war. Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators' discussions with Iran continue. “We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump, who insists the U.S. military remains in control of the conflict with a battered Iran. Yet, Tehran insists on several concessions from the U.S., which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks: ending the U.S. blockade on Iran’s ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon. Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 972 pounds of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%. Diplomatic efforts pick up following U.S. election A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Persian Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the U.S. military to carry out new strikes against Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defense officials after confirming earlier Friday that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to deescalate tensions. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also held phone calls with his Iraqi and Tunisian counterparts on Friday to discuss tensions in the region. Araghchi and Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein discussed Tehran’s vision for resuming negotiations with the U.S., according to Iraq’s News Agency. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, who held two calls with Araghchi this week, said Friday in a post on X that it was critical that both sides demonstrate “flexibility” to achieve the “compromise solutions” necessary to prevent the region from sliding into a new wave of escalation. Egypt’s top diplomat also held a phone call with his Emirati counterpart, Abdullah Bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to emphasize the importance of political negotiations to prevent another military confrontation that could fuel violence and destruction, according to a statement by Egypt’s Foreign Ministry.

articles.title: How the Iran war helped Democrats win the midterms
articles.summary: Tehran brought the costs of war into American homes, fuelling the backlash against Trump’s party.
articles.body:
This week, Iran’s response to the US-Israeli attacks led to one of the most dramatic political turnarounds in modern American history. Trump’s failed war on its own, however, is not why the Democrats pounded the Republicans and now control the Senate and House of Representatives for the next two years. Rather, it reflected and amplified many dynamics in American society that caused discontented, angry and fearful citizens to repudiate Trump’s Republicans and support Democrats.

The US president wrongly believed that his war on Iran would pummel the country into submission and turn it into a vassal state of the US and Israel. Iran survived, attacked the US, Israel and Arab lands, and brought the painful economic costs of war into every American home. It also humiliated Washington by revealing that America’s military prowess, like Trump’s behaviour and electoral promises, is erratic at best, and ineffective at worst.

The Iran war also sparked a cascade of consequences that hurt every American and, in some areas, exposed how national values such as democracy, equality and the rule of law, along with claims of global dominance, could prove illusory. Iran’s move with the greatest impact on ordinary Americans was restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up the prices Americans paid for groceries, gasoline, diesel, travel, most imports and other everyday necessities. Some 90 percent of voters said the cost of living was a major or crucial factor in how they would vote.

This was compounded by the inability of the US and Israel to force Iran to surrender, even after months of brutal attacks on political leaders, infrastructure, civilian and economic sites, and military installations. Instead, Iran’s counterattacks left US bases in the Arabian Peninsula and Jordan incapacitated or evacuated, and caused huge damage to Arab energy and transport systems, disrupting global energy flows and driving up prices. The balance of the war was clear after the first few weeks: the pain the US and Israel inflicted on Iran would be matched by pain in every household in the US and other countries that assisted in the attack on Iran.

Iran simultaneously exposed critical flaws in American militarism, leaving ordinary Americans confused, frustrated and often humiliated in different ways:

a) Trump ignored Americans’ repeatedly expressed opposition to attacking Iran, along with the constitutional requirement for congressional authorisation of war. CBS exit polls confirmed that voters opposed the war for both its useless militarism and its impact on the economy. The Trump administration’s disdain for both the law and ordinary Americans’ views angered many voters who took their constitutional rights more seriously than Trump did. Many voters rejected Republicans because Trump had insincerely promised in 2024 that he would end useless foreign wars.

b) More narrowly, Trump attacked Iran without clear, consistent or credible strategic goals; his main stated reason for attacking was to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, a prospect Israeli officials repeatedly told him was imminent, even though existing US and international inspections and intelligence assessments had repeatedly found no evidence of this.

c) When it dawned on Americans that Trump went to war mainly because Israel pushed him to do so, they reacted negatively in two ways. They felt humiliated that their country’s immense military power was unable to achieve its stated goals; they also felt angry and demeaned that a small, dependent, foreign country like Israel, with its extensive and sophisticated lobbying power in the US, could initiate this calamity that hurt American households and damaged US standing and credibility abroad.

Behind the anger, vulnerability and helplessness of most Americans who voted Democratic this week were deeper grievances that predated the Iran war. These included citizens’ fury at outrageous corruption in Washington; the privileged oligarchs, political donors, bankers and corporations that saw the US as their personal profit centre more than anything else; military and high-tech sectors that were out of control and threatened innocent lives; over-aggressive anti-immigration policing; and corporate media that seemed more interested in serving all of the above, and Israel, than in conveying truth and facts to the American people.

The election brought together voters’ household economic concerns with questions of national morality and foreign policy. Equally noteworthy, the day after the vote, Vice President JD Vance wrote on social media: “The reason we lost is the war.” He identified four demands among voters who had turned away from the Republicans: “End the war”, “Focus on the cost of living and inflation”, “Put America First” and “Change our relationship to Israel”.

An unprecedented aspect of this election and Iran’s policies has been the centrality of the US-Israeli genocide in Palestine to many progressive Democrats’ campaigns and to Iran’s approach to war and peace. Vance’s explicit mention of Israel was startling enough in a political system that, for nearly a century, has largely shaped its West Asia policies according to Israeli demands. Equally striking was President Trump’s last-minute promise, on election day, to end the nearly $4bn in US military aid to Israel. It was another insincere Trump con job meant to deceive voters, because the money would not stop flowing but would simply be channelled differently. It also emphasised the huge impact that conditions in Israel-Palestine and US complicity in the genocide had on voters.

articles.title: Jo Nabuurs lost his wedding ring while threshing grain on his family’s Dutch farm in the winter of 1942 or 1943; 83 years later, a man with a metal detector found it and returned it to his son, refusing a reward
articles.summary: A wedding ring that went missing on a Dutch farm during World War II has finally returned to its owner's family after 83 years.
articles.body: A wedding ring that went missing on a Dutch farm during World War II has finally returned to its owner's family after 83 years. The ring belonged to Jo Nabuurs, who lost it while threshing grain behind his family farm in the village of Odiliapeel in the winter of 1942 or 1943. He searched for it at the time but never managed to find it.Nabuurs had married in 1941, just a year or two before losing the ring. Despite his efforts to recover it, the ring remained buried on the farmland for decades. He later passed away without getting it back.According to Dutch broadcaster NOS, now, more than eight decades later, a man searching the area with a metal detector has found the missing ring. He discovered it about 20 centimetres below the ground in Odiliapeel, a village in the Dutch province of North Brabant.The discovery eventually reached Jo Nabuurs' family through a relative who lives near their former home. After hearing about the find, the relative contacted Jo's son, Bert Nabuurs, and told him that someone would be visiting him.The man who found the ring then personally brought it back to the family. Bert said he was surprised by the unexpected discovery, especially because the ring had been missing for so long. He also offered the finder a reward, but the man refused to accept any payment.Son recognises father's wedding ringFor Bert, the return of the ring brought back memories of his father and the story of how the family had lost the wedding jewellery.He told Dutch broadcaster DTV Nieuws that he had heard about the missing ring from his father. However, he had never seen him wearing it. Since Jo had lost the ring before Bert could remember, he had known his father only without a wedding band on his ring finger."My father sometimes told me that he had lost his ring," Bert said, as reported by Dutch broadcaster NOS.Although the ring had spent more than eight decades underground, the family had little difficulty establishing who it belonged to. Its inside carried an engraving of Jo and his wife's wedding date.This detail confirmed that the ring was the same one Jo had lost while working behind the farm. The engraved date also connected the recovered object directly to his parents' marriage in 1941.Bert said the family was delighted that the ring had finally been found. His brothers and sisters were particularly happy about its return after so many years. "My brothers and sisters think it's fantastic that the ring has been found," he said.Bert also said he had asked whether the man wanted a reward for finding and returning the family heirloom. However, the finder declined the offer. "I thought it was quite unusual. I even asked whether he wanted a reward, but he didn't."Family receives ring in good conditionApart from the engraved wedding date, the condition of the ring was another detail that pleased the family. Despite spending 83 years buried underground, it had remained in good condition.Bert said the ring had always been kept dry, which helped explain why it had survived so well. "The ring is still in good condition. It has always been kept dry," he said.The family was happy to have the ring back, even though Jo was no longer alive to see its return. For his children, the discovery brought back an object connected to their parents' marriage and a story their father had occasionally shared with them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘Every person has their luck’: Morocco’s beach metal detectorists
articles.summary: For many, the search is driven less by profit than by the thrill of an unexpected discovery.
articles.body:
Agadir, Morocco – Mustapha Harmouch moves slowly across the sand at Agadir’s Corniche, sweeping his metal detector in low, even arcs. He tunes out the surfers paddling beyond the shore, the children shrieking in the waves and the chatter of families, all his attention is on one sound: the beep that means the coil has passed over something buried beneath the sand.

For the 33-year-old content creator, that uncertainty is the whole appeal. The detector does not distinguish between treasure and rubbish, it gives the same signal whether the object below is a coin, a ring, a discarded piece of aluminium, or an old piece of fishing equipment.

“The excitement comes partly from not knowing what lies beneath the sand,” he told Al Jazeera English.

Harmouch bought a Tianxun TX 850 metal detector online about four years ago. What began as a hobby has since become an occasional part of the videos he posts on Stofishing, a YouTube travel and spearfishing channel with roughly 123,000 subscribers.

“It’s a nice hobby because it’s the kind of exploration where I find something and learn something new,” he said. “Each outing is a chance to encounter something I would otherwise never have known about.”

That curiosity has led him to old coins, including some associated with historical periods and places such as the Al Haouz region and Fez.

In the coastal town of Sidi Ouassay, about 65km south of Agadir, he says he found one of his rarest hauls: 14 Moroccan falus, old bronze or copper coins, in a single spot.

Some were too damaged by salt and the passage of time for their markings to be easily read, but Harmouch says the oldest dates to 1289 on the Hijri calendar.

For Harmouch, the coins’ value lies less in their price than in what they reveal about the past.

“I just collect them as a memory,” he said with a glint in his eye.

In the same area, he once found what he thought was a meteorite, only to learn it was a common, inexpensive mineral.

“Before asking, I thought I had found the best discovery,” he said, laughing at the memory.

That sense of possibility and adventure is what keeps him returning to the beaches around Agadir.

Harmouch goes detecting about four times a month, often with fellow members of the Moroccan Association for Research and Exploration Enthusiasts. He favours Taghazout and Agadir’s Corniche, where there is less rubbish for his detector to pick up.

The beaches have yielded jewellery, Moroccan coins and foreign currency, including a French 20-franc silver coin.

The possibility of finding something valuable is still part of the appeal. He once found a small gold ring in Taghazout.

“I always try to identify and return valuable lost items to their rightful owners,” Harmouch says.

Morocco’s main legal framework for protecting historical monuments, archaeological sites, works of art and antiquities dates to Law 22-80, which regulates archaeological prospecting and the treatment of historical discoveries. The government has reiterated that unauthorised archaeological searches on land or at sea are prohibited.

Under the law, searches intended to uncover monuments or moveable objects of historic, archaeological, or anthropological importance require authorisation, while accidental discoveries are subject to reporting requirements.

If a non-archaeological activity uncovers monuments, coins, works of art, or antiquities, the discovery must be reported to authorities. The objects should not be damaged or moved, except where necessary to protect them.

Finding a modern coin lost by a holidaymaker is one thing; deliberately searching for archaeological material is another.

But on Morocco’s coastline, archaeologists say the context in which an object is found can be just as important as the object itself.

Underwater archaeologist Basma Oumaima explains why context matters: “Sometimes something as simple as a fragment of metal, a coin, or a small tool can become important because of where it was found and what was found around it”.

“That does not mean curiosity itself should be discouraged. Metal detectors themselves can actually be useful tools in archaeology when they are used as part of a proper archaeological survey, where every find is located, recorded and studied within its context”.

Harmouch says he respects the law. Members of the association carry identification, avoid private property and heritage sites and treat detecting as a hobby rather than a job. His source of income, he says, comes mainly from content creation and a fishing equipment store.

For Mohamed Botaib, metal detecting has never been his main source of income. A former sports coach currently looking for work, he searches beaches, forests and mountains as a hobby.

His finds have been modest: ordinary coins, Moroccan dirhams and rings.

For Jalal Zegnoune, another detectorist, removing unwanted metal is one of the hobby’s practical sides. His detector has produced coins, jewellery, glasses and watches, along with less glamorous finds, including rusted sardine-can fragments, nails and lost fishing gear.

“I remove such objects from the beaches because some can be dangerous to beachgoers,” he said.

Zegnoune works full-time as a maintenance technician in Casablanca and goes metal detecting when he’s free or for limited hours in the evening.

“I also enjoy meeting other people who practise the hobby and sharing the objects they find.”

“When we look at the beach, it’s not to find treasure,” Botaib says. “It’s also our way of contributing to keeping our beaches clean. We collect pieces of metal and aluminium that we find and throw them away.”

articles.title: Pope Leo in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
articles.summary: Pope Leo travels to Uruguay just three weeks after having surgery for lung cancer.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.

The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.

The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.

The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru , which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.

"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.

"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.

Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.

In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".

He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.

He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral.

Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.

On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.

The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

articles.title: Rising airport drone alerts raise safety concerns
articles.summary: Fuelled by cheaper prices and better technology, drone flights near airports pose a serious risk.
articles.body:
Flights at Jersey Airport were hit on 30 and 31 October after unauthorised drone activity was reported , leading to services being cancelled or diverted to other airports.

It is the latest of many incidents at airports around the world, so we asked the experts: 'What's going on and what are the rights of passengers?'

"You can go on to Amazon, you can buy relatively small drones for a couple of hundred pounds, if not less," said Daniel Clarke, chief technology officer at StirlingX which helps airport operators detect drones and locating the people flying them.

The growing popularity of low-cost drones is contributing to an increase in disruptions at airports across the UK and Europe, according to Clarke.

"Particularly over the last few years, we've seen more and more occurrences of drone incursions into airports," he said. "Not just in the UK, but across Europe."

He suggested some users may not realise the consequences of their actions.

"I suspect if this is, sort of, people doing it for non-malicious reasons, they're probably using the lowest cost systems, and they probably don't realise that they're having the impact that they're having," he said.

He also suggested greater education was needed for recreational drone users, arguing that many people who buy drones online may be unaware of the regulations governing how and where they can fly them.

In the UK, drones must stay below 400ft (120m), and 164ft (50m) away from people, and must never be flown over crowds. Pilots are expected to fly responsibly, keep their drone in sight and check for any restrictions before taking off.

Extra rules apply near airports, airfields, heliports and spaceports where Flight Restriction Zones protect the site. Drones are not allowed to fly inside one of those zones without permission.

The Civil Aviation Authority warns endangering an aircraft with a drone is a serious offence and can lead to prosecution.

UK and European drone regulations do not apply to the Channel Islands so Jersey, Guernsey, Sark and Alderney have their own air navigation rules .

Drones are not allowed to be flown within two nautical miles of Jersey, Guernsey and Alderney airports without permission.

The rise in drones being found near airports has come at the same time as seismic shifts in the technology.

Modern drones, or unmanned aerial vehicles, have benefited from advances originally developed for smartphones, including computing power, navigation systems and internet connectivity, the BBC's Bottom Line podcast heard in September .

The cost of the underlying technology has fallen dramatically, making drones cheaper and more accessible, and improvements in lithium-ion batteries have also allowed aircraft to stay in the air for longer periods.

As a result, drones have become a central part of modern warfare and are also being used for an array of civilian uses such as emergency response, monitoring infrastructure such as railways for faults, delivery of urgent medical supplies and even heavy duty tasks such as industrial cleaning.

The rise in drones being flown close to airports has also brought chaos for passengers.

For affected passengers the rules are clear, the airline has a duty of care to passengers in this situation.

Allana Wilckens, legal counsel for FlightRight, said airlines should contact passengers to explain when a flight had been delayed or cancelled and, where possible, provide the reason.

"If the flight is cancelled, the airline should provide alternative flights, alternative ways for the passenger to reach the destination," she said.

Wilckens said if no suitable flights were available, airlines should arrange other transport, including rail, coach or car travel.

"If they still say no, the passenger is allowed to book the flight by themselves, and ask for refund at a later date."

Passengers should keep records of all communication from the airline and retain receipts for any reasonable expenses they incurred themselves.

According to Wilckens, passengers facing delays of more than five hours or cancellations were entitled to meals, accommodation and transport.

"It is an obligation of the airline to care for the passenger that is stranded," she said.

Airlines often argued that drone incidents amounted to "extraordinary circumstances" because they were outside their control.

But Wilckens said passengers should not automatically accept an airline's refusal to pay compensation.

"It's very common, especially when there is an occasion, like a drone attack, that the airlines will say, you have no right to compensation because it wasn't our fault," she said.

"There are other options, there are avenues we can pursue in order to help assist them in getting their compensation."

The Regional and Business Airports Group has been contacted for comment. The group was established to provide a collective voice for airports with less than three million passengers per year.

Jersey, Guernsey and Alderney airports are members of the group.

Airports UK, the national trade association representing the interests of airports, declined to comment on arrangements to prevent drone incursions "for security reasons".

A UK government spokesperson said all threats to airspace security were taken "seriously".

"We are working across government to explore additional steps to protect sensitive sites," they said.

"This includes the use of counter-drone technology to detect and deter unauthorised activity around critical infrastructure, such as airports, prisons, and defence establishments."

articles.title: Christmas post dates set out for Channel Islands
articles.summary: Jersey and Guernsey Post issue advice about the last recommended dates to send letters and parcels.
articles.body:
People across the Channel Islands have until mid-December to post Christmas cards and gifts to the UK.

Jersey Post and Guernsey Post have both confirmed the last recommended dates to get letters, parcels and documents from the islands in the run-up to the festive period.

In Jersey, the last recommended date for cards and parcels to the UK and Isle of Man is 15 December if using the tracked and signed service, while non-track and signed post can be sent by 11 December.

Residents of Guernsey have been advised to post letters to the UK by 17 December - or 18 December if using special delivery - and parcels to the UK, Jersey and Isle of Man by 14 December.

For deliveries going between the islands, Jersey Post said its last recommended date for letters and cards to Guernsey was 21 December while parcels could be sent on the same day if track and signed.

Parcels which do not use the track and signed service are recommended to be sent by 18 December.

It added letters going to addresses in Jersey should be sent by 22 December, but collections would also be made from the Broad Street and Rue des Pres post boxes the following day at 18:00 GMT.

Parcels going to addresses around the island should be posted by 22 December, Jersey Post said.

Post heading to European destinations from Jersey had a recommended last date of 26 November and 24 November for the rest of the world.

Guernsey Post said its last recommended posting date for letters and parcels across the island was 22 December.

It added letters and parcels could be sent to Sark addresses up to 16 December.

In Alderney, Guernsey Post said the last recommended date was 14 December for parcels and 18 December for letters.

Special deliveries can be made on 18 December for the UK and 16 December for Jersey and Isle of Man, but post which required UK customs clearance neede to be sent by 30 November.

articles.title: 'I went from home baking to winning on an international TV show'
articles.summary: Two baker friends have recently won an international TV baking competition.
articles.body:
Two baker friends who started making cakes in their home kitchen have now won an international TV competition.

Dusica Roberts, from Burnham-on-Sea in Somerset, and Verity Malinowska from Plymouth, took part in the TV series Bake Master Battles, a show on the Canadian Food Network.

The pair said winning the Halloween-themed episode, where they baked a zombie cake sculpture, was a "surreal" and "exciting" experience, as first reported by Burnham-on-Sea.com.

"As a child, you don't think, 'I'm going to make cakes when I'm older and go on international television'," Roberts said.

Roberts was a chef before she had children and then decided to bake for them in her home kitchen.

About 15 years ago, she decided to start a cake business, called Dusi-Cake.

She then met Malinowska about 10 years ago at a baking competition hosted in Birmingham.

The pair hit it off and began baking together. They described appearing on the show together as a "very exciting.

"Even being at the airport at 06:00 is very exciting, because me and Dusica absolutely love each other, we just have the most fun," Malinowska said.

"The show itself is amazing, they ran it so smoothly, we really felt we were looked after.

"It's quite intense on set but they just made you feel really welcome and really at ease."

The first challenge of the show saw the pair bake a cupcake display in 45 minutes, while the second was a three-hour battle to create a zombie cake sculpture.

"That could normally take days. Making it in three hours was a lot," Roberts said.

"It was intense. Luckily, Verity and I work really well together.

"We don't even really need to talk to each other, we just naturally come together."

articles.title: Long-lost Pepys board game found in attic
articles.summary: The Stop or Go game is now on display at the Museum of Board Games in Newent.
articles.body:
A rare prototype of a board game - described by a museum curator as a holy grail - has been discovered in an attic amidst a box of childhood toys.

Stop or Go, a road safety game played on a grid with counters, was designed in the 1940s by the games company Pepys, but was never manufactured.

Heidi Gibbs found what is believed to be a pre-production version of the game amidst her late grandmother's belongings and approached the Museum of Board Games in Newent in the Forest of Dean.

Curator Tony Boydell confirmed it was "the rarest Pepys game by a mile" as the game was known about but had never been seen. It has now been bought by the museum and is on permanent display.

Boydell said even the most knowledgeable "guru" of the company's archive, Rex Pitts, who wrote a book about the history of Pepys, had never seen a copy.

"It became very clear that this is something of a holy grail, it's a real treasure," he said.

Players throw the dice and move counters along the squares to the finishing line, choosing whether to obey the Highway Code or take a chance.

Boydell said he believed the game may have been discarded because it involved an element of risk-taking.

"For a small museum, to be able to get hold of something unique within the history of the games of a major British publisher is really unique," he added.

Gibbs, from Norfolk, said the game had stood out amongst her grandmother's toys due to its age.

"It looked very old-fashioned, but in a very good condition as well," she said.

"I contacted someone to do with Pepys board games and he had a look at it and said, 'obviously that is the exact game that is missing'. I thought it was absolutely amazing."

Gibbs said she decided to sell the game to the museum because she wanted board game fans to be able to "see and appreciate" it.

The mystery remains, though, as to how the game ended up in her grandmother's attic, as the family has no connection to Pepys.

Board game fans and collectors of Pepys memorabilia reacted with "real warmth" to the discovery, according to Boydell.

Philip Dennis, 73, from Aberystwyth in West Wales, said board games "tell us a lot about our social history".

"My games collection from the 1750s onwards contains a lot that were just played on Sundays because they were educational and so they were permitted," he said.

"Modern games are totally different to old games, but I think it's interesting to see how they've developed over the years," Dennis added.

articles.title: Period products essential not optional, public health director says
articles.summary: Matt Tyrer is working on a scheme which will ensure access to free sanitary towels or tampons.
articles.body:
Sanitary towels and tampons are "basic health and hygiene products" which are "essential and not optional", the public health director has said.

Matt Tyrer's department is spearheading the rolling out of a scheme which will see women and girls on the Isle of Man access free period products.

The Period Products (free provision) Act bill was introduced by MHK Joney Faragher as a private members bill in 2024. It has now been given Royal Assent but it will not come into force until October 2027.

Tyrer said making the products available would also ensure women or girls will not have to miss school, work or everyday activities.

Making them available to households on low incomes, he said, ensured women, girls and those who menstruate, can access them.

"We want to ensure people who need them have access to them as these are basic health and hygiene products that are essential and not optional," said Tyrer.

The scheme follows similar programmes in Scotland and Northern Ireland.

One of the co-founders of the Manx Menstrual Movement, Rhian Evans described Royal Assent as "a long time coming".

In 2023, Evans and Nicki Gaskell created the movement after speaking about period poverty and the basic right to have access products.

They then set up donation stations across the island as well as a pick and mix station at Douglas City Library.

They praised MHK Joney Faraghar, who they approached in 2024, saying she had done "a lot of work behind the scenes for this".

Evans said the pick and mix station started as an interim solution but they hoped it would continue.

"It is so important, it is also bittersweet because it also highlights that there is period poverty here and we wholeheartedly believe that your financial background does not matter, anyone who menstruates, should have this access," she said.

Becky Rolwey, head of public health communities, said the organisation would now engage with people to understand the needs going forward.

"We really want to ensure that people aren't embarrassed to access it, be it a father or brother or even a male friend and that they can get it easily," she said.

Rolwey said over the next year public health needed to determine the best and most sustainable products it could make available.

"Some people say a pad only costs X amount and is really cheap, but we know that those are not sufficient for everybody's needs," she said.

While exact locations on where the products could be found are not yet available, Tyrer said local authorities, schools, libraries, the Isle of Man Foodbank and other charities could potentially be used.

He added: "Fundamentally we want anybody who needs period products to be able to access them in a place that is convenient and appropriate."

articles.title: Houston mayor curbs cooperation of US city’s police with ICE
articles.summary: People stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
articles.body:
The mayor of Houston, the most populous city in the US state of Texas, has ordered the city’s police force to sharply limit its cooperation with the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

John Whitmire’s executive order came on Friday, days after Democrats swept statewide offices in the traditionally Republican state.

According to the order, Houston police will contact ICE only when a person is being arrested for a jailable offence, according to the Reuters news agency.

Whitmire said he had consulted Texas’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller before acting, and that the move was meant to reduce fear and anxiety across the city.

“Elections matter,” Whitmire told reporters. “I do this to begin a healing process,” he said, adding he hoped his executive order would become a model for other Texas cities.

Joining Whitmire at the news conference, Houston Police ⁠Chief J Noe Diaz said he supported the change and that his department had already begun to implement the new policy.

Under the new rules, people stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred to ICE simply because they have an administrative immigration warrant.

The decision reverses a policy Whitmire put in place in April under pressure from outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott.

Abbott had threatened to withdraw about $110m in state public safety grants, arguing that a city council ordinance limiting police contact with ICE breached Senate Bill 4, a 2017 state law that bars local police from restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also sued the mayor, the city council and the police chief over the ordinance.

“We’re taking an interpretation of the law today, working with the newly elected members of the state leadership, in implementing this policy,” Whitmire told reporters. “We don’t want people to worry about ⁠their workers, their family members, their students.”

The issue has drawn intense scrutiny in Houston. The Houston Chronicle found that city police contacted ICE at least 107 times in the first eight months of 2025, compared with nine times in the whole of 2024.

FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights group, called the order a victory for the city but said it was long overdue. “Today Houston won. Today our community can breathe easier,” FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said in a statement to KPRC.

Whitmire said he expected Houston’s approach to become a model for other cities. In Austin, Mayor Kirk Watson asked city officials on Friday to revise their own policy on ICE warrants.

articles.title: Why death of tribal activist Nisha Bhagat has sparked row in Jharkhand
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The death of tribal activist Nisha Kumari Bhagat, who allegedly died by suicide at her Ranchi residence on Friday, has triggered a political
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The death of tribal activist Nisha Kumari Bhagat, who allegedly died by suicide at her Ranchi residence on Friday, has triggered a political storm in Jharkhand. Opposition parties have accused the Hemant Soren-led government and police administration of failing to protect her despite repeated complaints of harassment. The controversy has intensified following an emotional Facebook Live broadcast in which Bhagat, visibly distressed and in tears, accused land brokers and people associated with the government of harassing her. She also alleged that her attempts to seek protection from the authorities had gone unanswered.In the nearly 11-minute video, which was viewed by thousands, Bhagat spoke about the threats she allegedly faced, apologised to her parents and expressed despair over her inability to fight the administration. Her death has prompted the BJP to demand a CBI investigation and chief minister Hemant Soren's resignation. The CPI(ML) Liberation, an ally of the ruling government, has also called for a fair investigation, while tribal organisations and local leaders have demanded accountability.The Soren govt responded to BJP's allegation admitting that though Bhagat was critical of the JMM govt she was not an "enemy"."Several land mafias and land brokers are BJP office-bearers, including prominent leaders. She may have criticised our party and government, but she was not our enemy. She was an Adivasi daughter of Jharkhand. The circumstances that led her to take this extreme step must be investigated. Police should examine her CDR details and the post-mortem report. Our police are conducting an impartial investigation, and action will be taken against whoever is found guilty. Let the preliminary police report come in the next two to four days," JMM central spokesperson Manoj Pandey said.The incident has particularly angered tribal communities, with members planning a symbolic protest ahead of her last rites at her ancestral village Uru in Gumla district on Saturday.What did Nisha Bhagat allege?In her final Facebook Live broadcast, Bhagat alleged that speaking out against the state government and land brokers could put people's lives at risk. She also claimed that despite repeatedly approaching the police and seeking security, she had received no meaningful assistance."I should have understood this earlier... People say there is BJP, there is Congress, but there is no one... My parents will be deeply hurt. My father played his role in the Jharkhand agitation. I tried very hard to fight the administration and also tried to talk to them about security... But today I have to embrace my own death because this Hemant Soren government can humiliate women, and I cannot bear this," she said.Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto said Bhagat had approached several people, including police officers, political representatives and social organisations, for help. He called for a comprehensive CBI investigation to establish whether complaints were ignored and identify those responsible.Her father, Handu Bhagat, also demanded a central investigation, alleging that influential people were involved. "I demand a high-level inquiry into my daughter's death. The probe should be conducted by the CBI, because high-profile people are involved," he told reporters.Ranchi Rural SP Gaurav Goswami said an Unnatural Death (UD) case had been registered and that forensic evidence had been collected from her residence. A medical board conducted the post-mortem examination."Everything is currently under investigation. We are looking into every point you have raised; however, it would be inappropriate to comment on any specific detail before the investigation is complete. Once the investigation concludes, all findings will be shared with you," Goswami said, responding to allegations of police negligence.Who was Nisha Bhagat?Nisha Kumari Bhagat was a tribal activist from Jharkhand who had raised her voice against alleged injustice, starvation, religious conversion and land grabbing. She was particularly vocal against land brokers and what she described as harassment of tribal communities.According to Jharkhand BJP president Aditya Sahu, Bhagat had consistently spoken against exploitation and oppression but received no support from the government. He questioned why the police had failed to intervene despite thousands watching her distress broadcast.Union minister of state for Defence Sanjay Seth also accused the state administration of failing to act, demanding the arrest of the Pithoria police station officer-in-charge, whom Bhagat had allegedly accused of ignoring her complaints."The death of Nisha by suicide is a grim reflection of the crumbling law and order situation in Jharkhand," Seth said, reiterating the demand for a CBI probe.The case shares an eerie similarity to the killing of Bharat Bhushan Tiwari, whose death in a controversial police encounter in Bihar has sparked widespread outrage. A video apparently showing the 28-year-old activist throwing away his pistol moments before being shot has raised allegations that he was killed after surrendering. Amid mounting political pressure, the Bihar government had ordered a judicial inquiry led by a retired High Court judge and suspended four police personnel pending investigation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Gurgaon law firms flout 50% WFH rule imposed to curb pollution, disgruntled employees tip off CAQM, inspections find 160 of 262 Trilegal staff and 87 of 117 JSA employees in office; both firms get showcause notices
articles.summary: GURGAON: Two law firms in the city were issued showcause notices for violating the 50% work from home directive currently in force in Delhi-NCR.
articles.body: GURGAON: Two law firms in the city were issued showcause notices for violating the 50% work from home directive currently in force in Delhi-NCR. Disgruntled employees, not administrative alacrity, are believed to have precipitated the move - sources said inspections were conducted at the premises of the firms on Nov 5 after the attendance rule "breach" was reported from within to Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM).The 50% attendance rule, along with a complete ban on construction, is in effect from Nov 5-20 as part of CAQM's pollution mitigation measures for the period when the air quality index is usually at its worst.The Nov 5 inspections found 160 of Trilegal's 262 employees present at its offices on the 18th and 19th floors of Godrej GCR. At JSA Advocates & Solicitors' offices on the ninth floor of the same building, 87 of 117 employees were physically present.Issued by the subdivisional magistrate (SDM) Badshapur, the notices are the first time penal provisions have been invoked in Delhi-NCR for WFH violation since the mandate came into force on Nov 5.The SDM sought an explanation of the breach from the firms within 24 hours, along with supporting documents, biometric attendance records, the roster implementing the WFH arrangement and details of employees permitted to work from home."The firms were warned that failure to respond within the stipulated period, or an unsatisfactory explanation, could invite proceedings under Section 14 of CAQM Act, 2021 and other applicable laws," said deputy commissioner Uttam Singh. Penalties under this section amount to imprisonment up to 5 years, a fine up to Rs 1 crore, or both.A representative of Trilegal said more than 50% of its employees were present because a puja was being conducted in the office. A JSA official said those present included employees, clients and visitors. Both firms said they would submit detailed responses to the administration.SDM Sanjeev Singla said inspections were conducted at five firms and violations were found only at these two. While the CAQM directive makes an exception for essential services, industry representatives in the city said it should be a non-binding directive. articles.title: AI images in property listings is false advertising, house-hunters say
articles.summary: One prospective buyer says it is like going to buy a new Mercedes but ending up with an old Skoda.
articles.body:
Property buyers and renters say the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in listings appearing on sites like Rightmove is "false advertising" and wastes time for all involved.

Jessica Otterwell, who is hunting for a flat in Brighton, East Sussex, told the BBC: "It's like if you went to buy a car because the picture was of a brand-new Mercedes and you turned up and it was a Skoda with one wheel."

An estate agent in Sussex said it could cost up for £50,000 to stage a property with furniture, while another in Surrey added: "Technology should help people, not deceive them."

Rightmove, a portal website which pulls in listings from other estate agents, and does not sell or rent properties directly, said AI-generated imagery was allowed on the site if it was clearly labelled.

The BBC has seen some property listings in which the images have been watermarked "Virtually staged" or "Artificially enhanced", but many others have not been disclosed.

The practice has been dubbed by some as "housefishing".

Otterwell, who compared the use of AI in property listings to catfishing on a dating app , said she had excitedly told her parents about a potential property to purchase, but "was greeted with what I can only describe as an absolute hovel".

"There was nothing apart from a stained mattress on the floor. It was in a terrible state of disrepair," she said.

"You walked in and thought 'where are the painted walls, the Matisse artwork, the fitted kitchen'."

Leyla Ledwith, 31, who was searching for a rental property in Brighton for three months, said that only two of the dozen properties she viewed had the furnishings seen on Rightmove.

"It is false advertisement, it is totally off-putting and really frustrating," she said.

"You see a lovely, modern property with nice furnishings. But you go and it's dark, dingy and everything is old and falling apart."

Ledwith said that it was wasting time for renters and buyers, sellers and landlords, and the estate agents.

"I don't understand who is benefiting from the AI photos," she added.

Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association, said it was concerning that some felt misled.

"It is absolutely crucial that listings sites, when integrating AI into their operations, apply the technology responsibly to avoid causing confusion for users at any point in the process," he said.

The BBC approached a number of estate agents for comment about their use of AI-generated images in listings.

David Vaughan, director of Sussex-based estate agents Aston Vaughan, said the firm used AI staging to "solve a problem for both sides".

"For owners, it's a huge cost saving – physical staging can cost anywhere from £5,000 on average up to £50,000 just to show a property with furniture in," he told the BBC.

"And buyers have told us empty rooms are hard to read for scale, and virtually dressing a room makes it much easier to understand how you would actually live in it."

Meanwhile, Warren Powell-Richards, an estate agency based in Surrey and Hampshire, says the future of the industry will involve AI.

"The challenge for estate agents is ensuring they don't get carried away with the possibilities at the expense of the customer experience," it said.

"We are not anti-AI. Taking that position would be madness in a world that's becoming increasingly dependent on it. However, we believe that it's a tool, and not a substitute for trust."

A spokesperson from Miles & Barr, an estate agent based in East Kent, said the use of AI and CGI to help prospective buyers and tenants visualise a property had been common practice for some time.

Rightmove said agents were responsible for the content they uploaded.

"It's critically important that people see accurate representations of properties on our platform," a spokesperson added.

"We take action where images are found to be misleading, including requiring amendments, removing the listing from our platform and taking further action where necessary."

articles.title: ‘Complete hooliganism': Mamata on attack at Abhishek Banerjee’s house ahead of Kali Puja
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee on Saturday reacted to the alleged attack on Trinamool Congress (TMC) national general
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee on Saturday reacted to the alleged attack on Trinamool Congress (TMC) national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee’s residence, accusing the BJP of disrupting traditional Kali Puja celebrations in the locality ahead of Kali Puja and Diwali.Speaking in Kolkata, Mamata questioned the disturbance caused in an area that serves as a traditional route for several Kali Puja processions.“Tomorrow is Kali Puja and Diwali. Last night, at 2:00 AM, an attack was carried out at Abhishek Banerjee’s house. This is our locality, a route through which many processions of Goddess Kali pass. Why are you causing such a disturbance?” she said.She also alleged that permissions for traditional pujas had been revoked while new celebrations were being allowed, and claimed that local clubs had been prevented from carrying out their activities the previous night.“We are part of the 'INDIA' alliance, and this is the reason for their anger,” Mamata added, alleging that the political opposition was behind the hostility.In another statement, Mamata said: “If you have the courage to use a bulldozer, why do you come here at 3:00 in the morning with a gang of thugs to attack a Kali Puja celebration?”The remarks came after Abhishek Banerjee alleged that BJP workers attacked his residence around 2am on Saturday, accusing Kolkata Police of failing to prevent the incident.In a post on X, Abhishek claimed the attack took place shortly after he released a video showing unidentified individuals allegedly conducting reconnaissance of his office and residence. He described it as the seventh attempt on his life in the past six months and accused the police and judiciary of failing to act.The BJP rejected the allegations, with West Bengal minister Dilip Ghosh dismissing them as an attempt to mislead people.“This is the first time we’ve seen a politician’s birthday being celebrated on the footpath. If someone creates a disturbance, there is bound to be a backlash. Besides, who has the time to kill Abhishek Banerjee? There is nothing left for them to say or do, so they are attempting to mislead people by bringing up this issue,” Ghosh said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
